{{Short description|Concept in education theory}}
{{about|knowledge spaces in mathematical psychology|the concept studied by philosopher Pierre Lévy|Knowledge space (philosophy)}}
In [[mathematical psychology]] and [[education theory]], a '''knowledge space''' is a [[Combinatorics|combinatorial]] [[Data structure|structure]] used to formulate [[mathematical model]]s describing the progression of a human [[Learning|learner]].<ref>{{citation|title=Knowledge Spaces|last1=Doignon|first1=J.-P.|last2=Falmagne|first2=J.-Cl.|author2-link=Jean-Claude Falmagne|publisher=Springer-Verlag|year=1999|isbn = 978-3-540-64501-6}}.</ref> Knowledge spaces were introduced in 1985 by [[Jean-Paul Doignon]] and [[Jean-Claude Falmagne]],<ref>{{citation |last1=Doignon |first1=J.-P. |title=Spaces for the assessment of knowledge |journal=International Journal of Man-Machine Studies |volume=23 |issue=2 |pages=175–196 |year=1985 |doi=10.1016/S0020-7373(85)80031-6 |last2=Falmagne |first2=J.-Cl. |author2-link=Jean-Claude Falmagne}}.</ref> and remain in extensive use in the education theory.<ref>{{citation |last1=Falmagne |first1=J.-Cl. |title=Knowledge Spaces. Applications in Education |year=2013 |publisher=Springer |last2=Albert |first2=D. |last3=Doble |first3=C. |last4=Eppstein |first4=D. |last5=Hu |first5=X. |author1-link=Jean-Claude Falmagne |author4-link=David Eppstein}}.</ref><ref>A [http://kst.hockemeyer.at/kst-bib.html bibliography on knowledge spaces] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161220143409/http://kst.hockemeyer.at/kst-bib.html |date=2016-12-20 }} maintained by Cord Hockemeyer contains over 400 publications on the subject.</ref> Modern applications include two [[Automated tutoring|computerized tutoring]] systems, [[ALEKS]]<ref>[http://wundt.uni-graz.at/MathPsych/cda/overview_sokrates.htm Introduction to Knowledge Spaces: Theory and Applications] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120208043055/http://wundt.uni-graz.at/MathPsych/cda/overview_sokrates.htm |date=2012-02-08 }}, Christof Körner, Gudrun Wesiak, and Cord Hockemeyer, 1999 and 2001.</ref> and the defunct [[RATH]].<ref>{{cite web |url=http://wundt.kfunigraz.ac.at/rath/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070630200637/http://wundt.kfunigraz.ac.at/rath/ |archive-date=2007-06-30  | title=Homepage of RATH }}</ref>

Formally, a knowledge space assumes that a domain of knowledge is a [[Set (mathematics)|collection]] of concepts or skills, each of which must be eventually [[Mastery|mastered]]. Not all concepts are interchangeable; some require other concepts as prerequisites. Conversely, [[Competence (human resources)|competency]] at one skill may ease the acquisition of another through similarity. A knowledge space marks out which collections of skills are ''feasible'': they can be learned without mastering any other skills. Under reasonable assumptions, the collection of feasible competencies forms the mathematical structure known as an [[antimatroid]].

Researchers and educators usually explore the structure of a discipline's knowledge space as a [[latent class model]].<ref>{{citation |last1=Schrepp |first1=M. |title=About the connection between knowledge structures and latent class models |journal=Methodology |volume=1 |issue=3 |pages=93–103 |year=2005 |doi=10.1027/1614-2241.1.3.93}}.</ref>

==Motivation==
Knowledge Space Theory attempts to address shortcomings of [[standardized test]]ing when used in educational [[Psychometrics|psychometry]]. Common tests, such as the [[SAT]] and [[ACT (test)|ACT]], compress a student's knowledge into a very small range of [[Ordinal data|ordinal]] [[Ranking|ranks]], in the process effacing the conceptual dependencies between questions. Consequently, the tests cannot distinguish between true understanding and [[Guessing|guesses]], nor can they identify a student's particular weaknesses, only the general proportion of skills mastered. The goal of knowledge space theory is to provide a language by which [[exam]]s can communicate<ref>{{cite arXiv |eprint=1511.06757 |class=math.CO |author1=Jean-Paul Doignon, Jean-Claude Falmagne |title=Knowledge Spaces and Learning Spaces |date=2015}}</ref> 
*''What the student can do'' and 
*''What the student is ready to learn''.

== Model structure ==
Knowledge Space Theory-based models presume that an [[Subject (documents)|educational subject]] {{Mvar|S}} can be modeled as a [[finite set]] {{Mvar|Q}} of [[concept]]s, skills, or topics. Each ''feasible state of knowledge'' about {{Mvar|S}} is then a [[subset]] of {{Mvar|Q}}; the set of all such feasible states is {{Mvar|K}}. The precise term for the information {{Math|(''Q'', ''K'')}} depends on the extent to which {{Mvar|K}} satisfies certain [[axiom]]s:

* A '''knowledge structure''' assumes that {{Mvar|K}} contains the [[empty set]] (a student may know nothing about {{Mvar|S}}) and {{Mvar|Q}} itself (a student may have fully mastered {{Mvar|S}}).  
* A '''knowledge space''' is a knowledge structure that is closed under [[Union (set theory)|set union]]: if, for each topic, there is an expert in a [[Form (education)|class]] on that topic, then it is possible, with enough time and effort, for each student in the class to become an expert on all those topics simultaneously.  
* A '''quasi-ordinal knowledge space''' is a knowledge space that is also closed under [[Intersection (set theory)|set intersection]]: if student {{Mvar|a}} knows topics {{Mvar|A}} and {{Mvar|B}}; and student {{Mvar|c}} knows topics {{Mvar|B}} and {{Mvar|C}}; then it is possible for another student {{Mvar|b}} to know only topic {{Mvar|B}}.  
* A '''well-graded knowledge space''' or '''learning space''' is a knowledge space satisfying the following axiom: <blockquote>If {{math|''S''∈''K''}}, then there exists {{math|''x''∈''S''}} such that {{math|''S''\{''x''}∈''K''}}</blockquote>  In educational terms, any feasible body of knowledge can be learned one concept at a time.

=== Prerequisite partial order ===
The more contentful axioms associated with quasi-ordinal and well-graded knowledge spaces each imply that the knowledge space forms a well-understood (and heavily studied) mathematical structure:

* A quasi-ordinal knowledge space can be associated with a [[distributive lattice]] under set union and set intersection. The name "quasi-ordinal" arises from [[Birkhoff's representation theorem]], which explains that distributive lattices [[Bijection|uniquely correspond]] to [[Partial order|partial orders]].
*A well-graded knowledge space is an [[antimatroid]], a type of mathematical structure that describes certain problems solvable with a [[greedy algorithm]].  
In either case, the mathematical structure implies that [[set inclusion]] defines [[Partial Order|partial order]] on {{Mvar|K}}, interpretable as an [[Curriculum#Higher education|educational prerequirement]]: if {{Math|''a''(⪯)''b''}} in this partial order, then {{Mvar|a}} must be learned before {{Mvar|b}}.

=== Inner and outer fringe ===
The prerequisite partial order does not uniquely identify a [[curriculum]]; some concepts may lead to a variety of other possible topics. But the [[covering relation]] associated with the prerequisite partial does control curricular structure: if students know {{Mvar|a}} before a lesson and {{Mvar|b}} immediately after, then {{Mvar|b}} must cover {{Mvar|a}} in the partial order. In such a circumstance, the new topics covered between {{Mvar|a}} and {{Mvar|b}} constitute the '''outer fringe''' of {{Mvar|a}} ("what the student was ready to learn") and the '''inner fringe''' of {{Mvar|b}} ("what the student just learned").

==Construction of knowledge spaces==
In practice, there exist several methods to construct knowledge spaces. The most frequently used method is querying experts. There exist several querying algorithms that allow one or several experts to construct a knowledge space by answering a sequence of simple questions.<ref>{{citation|title=Extracting human expertise for constructing knowledge spaces: An algorithm |last1=Koppen |first1=M. |journal=Journal of Mathematical Psychology|volume=37|pages=1–20 |year=1993 |doi=10.1006/jmps.1993.1001|doi-access=free }}.</ref><ref>{{citation|title=How to build a knowledge space by querying an expert |last1=Koppen |first1=M. |last2=Doignon |first2=J.-P. |journal=Journal of Mathematical Psychology|volume=34|issue=3|pages=311–331 |year=1990 |doi=10.1016/0022-2496(90)90035-8|doi-access=free |hdl=2013/ULB-DIPOT:oai:dipot.ulb.ac.be:2013/166478 |hdl-access=free }}.</ref><ref>{{citation|title=A simulation study concerning the effect of errors on the establishment of knowledge spaces by querying experts |last1=Schrepp |first1=M. |last2=Held |first2=T. |journal=Journal of Mathematical Psychology|volume=39|issue=4|pages=376–382 |year=1995|doi=10.1006/jmps.1995.1035}}</ref>

Another method is to construct the knowledge space by explorative data analysis (for example by [[item tree analysis]]) from data.<ref>{{citation|title=Extracting knowledge structures from observed data |last1=Schrepp |first1=M. |journal=[[British Journal of Mathematical and Statistical Psychology]]|volume= 52|issue=2 |pages=213–224 |year=1999|doi=10.1348/000711099159071}}</ref><ref>{{citation |title=A method for the analysis of hierarchical dependencies between items of a questionnaire |last1=Schrepp |first1=M. |journal=Methods of Psychological Research Online |volume=19 |pages=43–79 |year=2003 |url=http://www.dgps.de/fachgruppen/methoden/mpr-online/issue19/art3/mpr106_04.pdf |access-date=2009-07-16 |archive-date=2016-03-03 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160303173146/http://www.dgps.de/fachgruppen/methoden/mpr-online/issue19/art3/mpr106_04.pdf |url-status=dead }}</ref> A third method is to derive the knowledge space from an analysis of the problem solving processes in the corresponding domain.<ref>{{citation|title=Knowledge Spaces: Theories, Empirical Research, Applications|last1=Albert|first1=D.|last2=Lukas|first2=J.|publisher=Lawrence Erlbaum Associates, Mahwah, NJ|year=1999}}</ref>
